Alternative causes (Zenker diverticulum, anterior cervical osteophytes/DISH, peptic strictures, neoplasm) are less consistent: Zenker’s has posterior outpouching and regurgitation/halitosis and would have a different barium appearance; anterior osteophytes would be evaluated on lateral cervical x‑ray and would not produce a thin membranous web on esophagram; lower esophageal peptic strictures produce distal obstruction and neoplasm would often show mass effect or progressive symptoms and possibly palpable nodes (not present). Plummer‑Vinson syndrome (upper esophageal web with iron deficiency anemia) is a related consideration but requires hematologic data not provided. Given the imaging finding and clinical presentation, the single most likely diagnosis is a cervical/upper esophageal web causing mechanical (solids-predominant) dysphagia. 

[DIAGNOSIS] Upper (cervical) esophageal web causing mechanical solids-predominant dysphagia.

ANALYSIS: Incorrect. Plummer‑Vinson syndrome is a clinical syndrome (iron‑deficiency anemia, dysphagia from upper esophageal web, and mucosal changes). The prediction names only the anatomic lesion (a cervical esophageal web causing mechanical solids‑predominant dysphagia), which can occur independently of the full Plummer‑Vinson syndrome. Omitting the systemic/hematologic features means the two are not clinically equivalent.

VERDICT: INCORRECT
